front_blocks.md: Define **entropy**.

back_blocks.md: **Entropy** (*S*) is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy in a system. It is a measure of disorder: the greater the disorder, the higher the entropy.

cards.back_md: **Entropy** (*S*) is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy in a system. It is a measure of disorder: the greater the disorder, the higher the entropy.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Gases have greater entropy than liquids, which in turn have greater entropy than solids.

back_blocks.md: The order of entropy is: gas > liquid > solid. Gases are most disordered, solids are most ordered.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Gases have greater entropy than liquids, which in turn have greater entropy than solids.
cards.back_md:
**True.**

The order of entropy is: gas > liquid > solid. Gases are most disordered, solids are most ordered.

front_blocks.md: Explain why the decomposition of CaCO<sub>3</sub> results in an increase in entropy.

back_blocks.md: A **gaseous** CO<sub>2</sub> molecule is formed from a solid. Gases are far more disordered than solids, so the number of possible arrangements increases and **entropy** increases.

cards.front_md: Explain why the decomposition of CaCO<sub>3</sub> results in an increase in entropy.
cards.back_md:
CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

A **gaseous** CO<sub>2</sub> molecule is formed from a solid. Gases are far more disordered than solids, so the number of possible arrangements increases and **entropy** increases.

front_blocks.md: What happens to the entropy of a substance when it melts, and why?

back_blocks.md: Entropy increases when a substance melts. The regularly arranged **lattice** of particles becomes a more randomly arranged liquid in which particles can rotate and slide over each other, increasing **disorder**.

cards.front_md: What happens to the entropy of a substance when it melts, and why?
cards.back_md: Entropy increases when a substance melts. The regularly arranged **lattice** of particles becomes a more randomly arranged liquid in which particles can rotate and slide over each other, increasing **disorder**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Dissolving a solid in a solvent causes a decrease in entropy.

back_blocks.md: Dissolving a solid increases entropy. The particles spread out from the ordered solid lattice into a more disordered solution, increasing the number of possible arrangements.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Dissolving a solid in a solvent causes a decrease in entropy.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

Dissolving a solid increases entropy. The particles spread out from the ordered solid lattice into a more disordered solution, increasing the number of possible arrangements.

front_blocks.md: State the order of entropy for the three physical states of matter.

back_blocks.md: Gases have the **highest entropy** (most disordered) and solids have the **lowest entropy** (most ordered).

cards.front_md: State the order of entropy for the three physical states of matter.
cards.back_md:
gas > liquid > solid

Gases have the **highest entropy** (most disordered) and solids have the **lowest entropy** (most ordered).

front_blocks.md: When a system becomes more disordered, its **..........** increases.

back_blocks.md: When a system becomes more disordered, its **entropy** increases.

cards.front_md: When a system becomes more disordered, its **..........** increases.
cards.back_md: When a system becomes more disordered, its **entropy** increases.

front_blocks.md: Why does entropy decrease during crystallisation of a salt from solution?

back_blocks.md: During **crystallisation**, particles move from a disordered solution into a regular, ordered **solid lattice**. The number of possible arrangements decreases, so entropy decreases.

cards.front_md: Why does entropy decrease during crystallisation of a salt from solution?
cards.back_md: During **crystallisation**, particles move from a disordered solution into a regular, ordered **solid lattice**. The number of possible arrangements decreases, so entropy decreases.

Why is a negative value of Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> expected for the reaction 2Mg (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2MgO (s)?

back_blocks.md: A gas molecule (O<sub>2</sub>) is consumed and no gas is produced. The products are all **solid**, which is more ordered than the reactants. The number of possible arrangements decreases, so Δ*S*<sub>system</sub><sup>θ</sup> is **negative**.
